title: Joining the League of Nations, 1919
resolution: Historical question (1919): Should the United States Senate ratify the Treaty of Versailles and join the League of Nations?
summary: After World War I, President Woodrow Wilson championed a League of Nations to keep the peace. Senator Henry Cabot Lodge led the fight for reservations. The Senate's rejection shaped American foreign policy for a generation.

background.p: The Treaty of Versailles, signed in June 1919, ended World War I with Germany and included the Covenant of the League of Nations, an organization of countries meant to settle disputes and prevent war. President Woodrow Wilson had made the League the center of his peace plan. Under the Constitution, a treaty needs the approval of two-thirds of the Senate.

Republicans controlled the Senate after the 1918 elections, and Henry Cabot Lodge chaired the Foreign Relations Committee. His committee attached reservations to the treaty, most importantly limiting Article X, which committed members to preserve one another's territory against aggression. A smaller group of "irreconcilables" opposed the treaty in any form. Wilson refused to accept the reservations and urged his supporters to vote against the treaty with them; on November 19, 1919, the Senate rejected a peace treaty for the first time in its history, and a final attempt failed in March 1920. The United States never joined the League.

terms.def: An international organization founded in 1920 to promote peace; the forerunner of the United Nations.
The League Covenant's pledge that members would respect and preserve each other's territory and independence against external aggression.
A condition the Senate attaches to its approval of a treaty.
The idea that nations agree to treat an attack on one as a concern of all.
Senators who opposed the treaty in any form.

aff.label: Wilson's position (ratify)
aff.stance: Joining the League gives the world a way to prevent another catastrophic war, and America must lead it.

args.claim: Collective security can prevent future wars.
args.warrant: If nations pledge together to resist aggression, would-be aggressors will be deterred, as no country could act against all.
args.evidence: Wilson's speeches during his 1919 tour; the League Covenant.
args.response: Lodge's side answered that Article X could drag the U.S. into foreign conflicts without Congress's consent.

args.claim: Without America, the League will be weak.
args.warrant: The United States was the world's leading economic power; a League without it would lack the strength to act.
args.evidence: The relative economic and military strength of the major powers after 1918.
args.response: Opponents replied that America could cooperate with other nations case by case without binding commitments.

args.claim: The war's sacrifices demand a lasting peace.
args.warrant: After millions of deaths, nations have a duty to build institutions that make such a war less likely.
args.evidence: Casualty figures from World War I; Wilson's appeals to the war's purpose.
args.response: Opponents answered that a flawed treaty might sow future conflict rather than prevent it.

args.claim: Reservations would weaken the League's promise.
args.warrant: If the U.S. joined only with exceptions to its core pledge, other nations might add their own, and collective security would mean little.
args.evidence: Wilson's statements opposing the Lodge reservations.
args.response: Lodge's side replied that the reservations protected the Constitution's war powers and that other allies could accept them.

neg.label: Lodge's position (reservations or reject)
neg.stance: The treaty as written would commit America to wars without Congress's consent and limit its independence.

args.claim: Article X could commit the U.S. to war without Congress.
args.warrant: The Constitution gives Congress the power to declare war; an open-ended pledge to defend other nations' borders could override that.
args.evidence: Lodge's reservations, especially on Article X; Senate debates of 1919.
args.response: Wilson's side argued that Article X was a moral obligation, not an automatic legal command, and Congress would still decide.

args.claim: America should keep its independence in foreign affairs.
args.warrant: From Washington's Farewell Address on, American policy had avoided permanent alliances; the League would bind the country to others' disputes.
args.evidence: Washington's Farewell Address (1796); the Monroe Doctrine.
args.response: Wilson's side replied that the world had changed, and isolation hadn't kept America out of World War I.

args.warrant: A peace that imposed harsh terms and redrew borders by the victors' choices might cause future conflicts the League would then require America to fight.
args.evidence: Contemporary criticism of the treaty's terms.
args.response: Wilson's side argued that the League itself was the means to correct the treaty's flaws over time.

args.warrant: Approving the treaty with conditions that protect the Constitution would let America join while keeping its war powers; refusing compromise was the real cause of failure.
args.evidence: The Senate Historical Office's account of the 1919 votes and Wilson's refusal to negotiate.
args.response: Wilson's side held that the reservations gutted the treaty's central promise.

strawmen.strawman: Wilson wanted foreign countries to run America.
strawmen.why: Wilson argued for collective security among sovereign nations, with America leading.
strawmen.steelman: Collective security can deter aggression; the League needs American strength, and the war's sacrifices demand an institution to keep the peace.

strawmen.strawman: Lodge just hated Wilson and wanted to sabotage peace.
strawmen.why: Lodge and the reservationists offered to approve the treaty with conditions protecting Congress's war powers.
strawmen.steelman: Article X could commit America to war without Congress; reservations would protect the Constitution and American independence while allowing participation.

weak.arg: If the U.S. had joined, World War II would never have happened.
weak.why: A speculative counterfactual; historians debate the League's weaknesses beyond American absence.
An overstatement; even many reservationists supported cooperation with other nations.

aff: Would Article X require the U.S. to send troops without a vote of Congress?
Why not accept the reservations to get the treaty approved?
How would the League enforce its decisions?
neg: How would America prevent another world war without the League?
Did staying out of alliances keep the U.S. out of World War I?
Would other nations accept American reservations?
